faqs.question: Which Halloween songs work for a 2-year-old?
faqs.answer: Pick a tune your toddler already knows and give it new spooky words, such as "Sleepy Ghost" sung to "Frère Jacques". Friendly-monster recordings work too: Cookie Monster's "C Is for Cookie" (on record by 1974) and Raffi's "Spider on the Floor" (1976).

faqs.question: Which Halloween songs can preschoolers act out?
faqs.answer: Ring games and start-stop songs suit ages 4 to 7, like "The Witch Is in the Wood" sung to "The Farmer in the Dell". Instrumental pieces also work: sweep a pretend broom to Dukas's "The Sorcerer's Apprentice" (1897) or stomp to Mussorgsky's "The Hut on Fowl's Legs" (1874).

faqs.question: What Halloween songs do 8 to 12 year olds like?
faqs.answer: Older kids prefer recordings they recognise, such as "BAMM" from Disney's Zombies (16 February 2018), "Rotten to the Core" from Descendants (2015) or Imagine Dragons' "Bones" (11 March 2022). Older novelty songs like Jumpin' Gene Simmons's "Haunted House" (1964) go down well with this age too.

faqs.question: Is "Have You Seen the Ghost of John?" a traditional song?
faqs.answer: It is usually labelled traditional, but nobody has documented its author or first printing. The earliest copy we found in the Internet Archive's searchable books was a 1981 Silver Burdett school textbook, so treat its age as unknown rather than ancient.

faqs.question: Can I print Halloween song lyrics for my class?
faqs.answer: In the US, words published before 1931 are public domain, so Newell's 1883 rounds and the "Frère Jacques" tune can go on a song sheet. Lyrics from modern recordings such as a 2015 Disney song are still under copyright, so play them instead of printing them.

faqs.question: How loud should music be at a kids' Halloween party?
faqs.answer: The WHO puts normal conversation at about 60 dB and advises keeping devices below 60% of maximum volume. Its page sets no separate child limit, so for under-7s aim for conversation level and turn it down if you must raise your voice to reach a child at arm's length.

faqs.question: Does singing help toddlers learn songs and words?
faqs.answer: A 2026 Infancy study of 128 babies found that by 20 months, infants combine melody and lyrics when recognising a familiar song, and listened longest when one part was new. It did not measure vocabulary, so it supports new words on old tunes rather than proving a learning gain.

faqs.question: Which tunes can I borrow to write a Halloween song with my kids?
faqs.answer: Use public-domain tunes children already know: "Frère Jacques", "Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush" and "The Farmer in the Dell" all appear in collections printed well before 1931. Keep one action per line so toddlers can join in before they know the words.

faqs.question: Are there Halloween songs that aren't scary for little kids?
faqs.answer: Yes: songs where the monster is silly or small, like Grover's "Monster in the Mirror" (recorded 1990), avoid fright entirely. Saint-Saëns's "Fossils" turns skeletons into a xylophone joke rather than a scare.

faqs.question: Can I send my child or grandchild a Halloween card with a song?
faqs.answer: Yes. SubhSandesh's Halloween card has a kids tone with round, blushing ghosts and no jump scares, and plays a YouTube song you paste in or one of eight built-in favourites; the premium page adds a voice note up to 60 seconds, so you can sing to them yourself.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Songs for Kids by Age, From Toddlers to Age Twelve

The best Halloween songs for kids change with age: toddlers want a familiar melody with new spooky words, 4- to 7-year-olds want songs that tell them when to move and when to stop, and 8- to 12-year-olds want real recordings. Most of that music now comes out of a phone. On SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and 48.4% of views happen on a touch device, so a small speaker turned up too far is the usual way a sing-along goes wrong.

Below are 18 songs for Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027: four new verses written here for public-domain tunes, one chant game printed in 1883, four public-domain instrumental pieces, and nine recordings with the release year checked against MusicBrainz.

## What makes a Halloween song right for a child's age?

A good Halloween song for a child has a predictable melody and words that give them a job. Under-7s rarely need fright.

A [2026 Infancy study from the University of Toronto Scarborough](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13269233) played versions of "Wheels on the Bus" to 128 babies. In exploratory analyses, 11-month-olds made more rhythmic movements to the familiar words. The 20-month-olds listened longest when either the tune or the words was new, which is a good case for new Halloween words on an old melody.

| Age | Song type that works | Example (year) | What the research found |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | Old tune, new words, hand actions | "Sleepy Ghost" to "Frère Jacques" (tune c.1780) | 20-month-olds listened longest when words or tune were new (Dou et al., 2026) |
| 4–7 | Start-stop action songs and ring games | "The Witch Is in the Wood" (game printed 1883) | 16 music sessions raised teacher-rated self-control at ages 4–5 (Zhong and Pan, 2026) |
| 8–12 | Recorded novelty and film songs | "BAMM" (2018) | Not tested in either study; chosen for clean lyrics |
| Mixed ages | Instrumental pieces for movement | "The Sorcerer's Apprentice" (1897) | No lyrics competing with your instructions |

The table compares four age bands: the younger the child, the more the song should be one they could already sing.

## Ages 1 to 3: monster-friendly songs and new words to old tunes

Keep each song under two minutes, sing it three times in a row, and let the hands do the scary part.

### 1. "Sleepy Ghost" (new words to "Frère Jacques")

The tune is a French round usually traced to a manuscript from about 1780, long out of copyright. Tuck hands under one cheek for "sleepy", then throw them wide on "boo".

- Sleepy ghostie, sleepy ghostie,
- Wake up now, wake up now!
- Pumpkins all are glowing, pumpkins all are glowing,
- Boo, boo, boo! Boo, boo, boo!
- Little black cat, little black cat,
- Tiptoe out, tiptoe out,
- Moon is up and shining, moon is up and shining,
- Meow, meow, meow! Meow, meow, meow!

### 2. "The Mummy Walk" (new words to "Mulberry Bush")

William Wells Newell printed "As We Go Round the Mulberry Bush" in [*Games and Songs of American Children* (1883)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/45762), with a chore for each day of the week. This version swaps the chores for Halloween creatures.

- This is the way the mummy walks (arms straight out, stiff knees)
- This is the way the bat flaps (elbows flapping)
- This is the way the pumpkin rolls (hands rolling over each other)
- This is the way the ghost says boo (hide behind hands, then peek)
- All on a Halloween evening.

### 3. Three recordings with friendly monsters

The monster in each of these is silly, hungry or small, never frightening.

- **"C Is for Cookie"**, Cookie Monster (on record by 1974): a monster whose only goal is a biscuit.
- **"Monster in the Mirror"**, Grover (recorded 1990): good for a pull-a-face game at the mirror.
- **"Spider on the Floor"**, Raffi, *Singable Songs for the Very Young* (1976): a spider climbs the body part by part, so children point as it goes.

## Ages 4 to 7: action songs that start and stop

At this age the best Halloween song has a rule built in: move on the music, stop when it ends. A [2026 BMC Psychology trial with 67 children aged 4 and 5](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13188394) gave two music groups 16 sessions over 8 weeks, and the percussion group was reminded to stop the moment the music ended. Both groups outscored the control group on teacher-rated persistence, impulse control and waiting, though not on the "consciousness" scale.

### 4. "The Witch Is in the Wood" (new words to "The Farmer in the Dell")

Newell records "The Farmer in the Dell" as a New York street ring game: each child picks the next until "the cheese stands alone" and is clapped out. Here nobody is clapped out; the last child becomes the next witch.

- The witch is in the wood, the witch is in the wood,
- Heigh-ho, the owls all know, the witch is in the wood.
- The witch picks a cat... The cat picks a bat...
- The bat picks an owl... The owl picks a pumpkin...
- The pumpkin glows alone, the pumpkin glows alone,
- Heigh-ho, the owls all know, now you're the witch, go on!

### 5. "Ghost in the Cellar" (a chant game from 1883)

Newell has one child hide as the ghost while another plays the mother. The family calls, "Mother, I see a ghost," and she answers, "It was only your father's coat hanging up." For under-7s, hide the ghost behind a sofa, not in a dark cellar, and have everyone walk, not run, when it appears.

### 6. Four instrumental pieces for moving like a monster

Music without words leaves room for your instructions, and each piece suits one movement.

- **"The Sorcerer's Apprentice"**, Paul Dukas (premiered 18 May 1897): sweep an imaginary broom, faster and faster.
- **"The Hut on Fowl's Legs"**, from Modest Mussorgsky's *Pictures at an Exhibition* (1874): Baba Yaga's hut, so stomp on chicken legs.
- **"Fossils"**, from Camille Saint-Saëns's *The Carnival of the Animals* (written 1886, published 1922): xylophone for wobbly skeleton knees.
- ***The Skeleton Dance***, Walt Disney's 1929 cartoon: watch once, then copy the skeletons.

## Ages 8 to 12: novelty and film songs with the years checked

Older children want songs they have actually heard. Each year below comes from the song's MusicBrainz release record, cross-checked with its film where there is one.

- **"Haunted House"**, Jumpin' Gene Simmons (1964 single): novelty rock and roll about moving into a haunted house.
- **"Addams Groove"**, Hammer (single released 17 December 1991): the theme for the 1991 *Addams Family* film.
- **"Rotten to the Core"**, the *Descendants* cast (2015 Disney Channel film): villains' children enjoying being bad.
- **"I'm in Love with a Monster"**, Fifth Harmony (14 August 2015): from *Hotel Transylvania 2*.
- **"BAMM"**, Milo Manheim, Meg Donnelly and Kylee Russell (16 February 2018): the block-party song from Disney's *Zombies*.
- **"Bones"**, Imagine Dragons (11 March 2022): a stomping beat with clean lyrics.

### 7. "A Hallowe'en Rhyme" (a round printed in 1883)

Newell's New York round opens "Oh, dear doctor, don't you cry! Your true love will come by-and-by," then guesses a sweetheart's fortune from the colour they wear. In this costume-colour version, each child names a colour and the group sings the line.

- If your ghost comes dressed in green, that's the bravest ghost we've seen.
- If your ghost comes dressed in gray, that's a sign it's slipped away.
- If your ghost comes dressed in blue, it will share its sweets with you.
- If your ghost comes dressed in black, it's behind you, don't look back!

A correction: "Have You Seen the Ghost of John?" is usually labelled a traditional round, but our earliest Internet Archive hit was a 1981 Silver Burdett school music textbook we could not open. Author and date unknown, so its words are not printed here.

## Classroom rules: how loud, and what you can print

The [World Health Organization's safe-listening guidance (6 March 2026)](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/deafness-and-hearing-loss-safe-listening) puts a whisper at about 30 dB and conversation at about 60 dB. It rates 80 dB safe for up to 40 hours a week but 90 dB for only four, and advises keeping devices below 60% of maximum volume.

The WHO page sets no separate limit for children. For under-7s we suggest conversation level: if you must raise your voice to reach a child at arm's length, turn it down, and give children who cover their ears a quiet corner.

For song sheets, [Cornell University Library's copyright chart](https://guides.library.cornell.edu/copyright/publicdomain) lists US works published before 1931 as public domain. Recordings follow separate rules: those published before 1926 are free, while 1926–1946 recordings are protected for 100 years. So Newell's 1883 words and the "Frère Jacques" tune can go on a class sheet, but a 2015 Disney lyric cannot; other countries often count from the author's death, so check locally.

## Putting a song on a Halloween card for one child

A song can also go to one child far away. For a grandchild or a niece, the [interactive Halloween card with a kids mode](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about five minutes. Its kids tone keeps the ghosts round and blushing with no jump scares, and it plays a YouTube song you paste in or one of eight built-in Halloween favourites.

To sing "Sleepy Ghost" yourself, the [premium Halloween page with a 60-second voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about ten minutes, holds up to 12 photos and, for kids, never shows a No button. SubhSandesh pages average 11.1 views each, so a song on one is rarely heard once. For another occasion, [browse every SubhSandesh template](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

## When a song or a card is the wrong choice

Both Halloween pages are built for one recipient and run in English only, so a class of 25 is better served by a speaker and a song sheet.

A child who hates loud noise is better served by a quiet humming game. For a 2-year-old, a live "Sleepy Ghost" on your lap beats any screen, and it takes about 90 seconds.

## Sources

- Dou, Withers, Wedderburn and Cirelli, *Infancy*, 2026 (melody and lyrics in song recognition).
- Zhong and Pan, *BMC Psychology*, 14 April 2026 (music activities and preschool self-control).
- World Health Organization, "Deafness and hearing loss: Safe listening", 6 March 2026.
- William Wells Newell, *Games and Songs of American Children*, Harper & Brothers, copyright 1883 (Project Gutenberg).
- Cornell University Library, "Copyright Term and the Public Domain", as of 1 January 2026.
